The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1) isn’t about kicking families off Medicaid—it’s about stopping the bleeding. Medicaid lost $55B last year alone to fraud and improper payments while ER misuse by non-citizens drained resources meant for vulnerable Americans.

The bill’s structural reforms—like phasing down state-directed payments to Medicare rates and reducing the 90% federal reimbursement for emergency services to unauthorized immigrants—prioritize accountability. CBO estimates $1.15T in savings by cutting bureaucratic waste and enforcing work requirements for able-bodied adults.

Protecting Medicaid means funding care for those who need it, not subsidizing systemic abuse. Real reform requires hard choices—this bill makes them.

Congressman Baird’s focus on crop insurance and biofuels is spot-on. The 2025 Farm Bill (H.R.1) finally modernizes safety nets with higher reference prices and crop insurance subsidies—critical for farmers facing volatile markets. But let’s not ignore the $294B SNAP cuts buried in the same bill.

Redirecting funds from bloated food stamp bureaucracy to actual agricultural innovation? Smart. Year-round E15 and biofuel support align with Trump’s energy dominance agenda, but the real win is forcing states to share SNAP costs.

Ag groups cheer, but taxpayers should demand deeper cuts to D.C.’s welfare-industrial complex.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R.1) does lock in critical tax relief for farmers, but let’s cut through the confetti. Section 10401 allocates $2.8B for disaster programs while Section 3 of Title VII permanently inflates the estate tax exemption to $15M—good for generational farms.

Yet buried in Title I’s $65.6B agricultural spending spree, bureaucrats carved out $1.8B in conservation cuts and redirected $450M from forestry grants to pet projects. Crop insurance subsidies jump 3-5% (Section 201), but Washington’s addiction to layering complexity onto programs like ARC and PLC guarantees more administrative bloat.

Real victory? Locking the 20% QBI deduction. The rest? A mixed harvest of needed relief and classic D.C. waste.
